Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak against Bill C-43. This is an act to recriminalize abortion.
I feel that this bill is the very height of government hypocrisy. The bill would jail medical doctors for two years for performing a medical service, unless vaguely defined health criteria enshrined in criminal law are met. Women are also liable for criminal penalties under Section 21 of the Criminal Code for aiding and abetting in the commission of a crime. Abortion under circumstances described by several Supreme Court justices as valid reasons to have an abortion will now be one such criminal offence.
I understand the pressure that the government is under. Some people have called for criminal legislation in this area. The Leader of the Official Opposition, the Leader of the Liberal Party, has called for criminal legislation in this area. Several ministers and backbenchers have called for criminalization on abortion.
Some think that this bill should be a free vote because they say that it is a matter of conscience for the members of this House of Commons to decide. I believe that it is a matter of conscience for each individual woman to decide, not for the members of this House.
The Minister of Justice in his justifications for this bill said this legislation would prevent people who are not doctors from performing an abortion. This is an example of the hypocrisy that I have spoken about.
Government Orders
The Criminal Code already deals with the performance of surgical procedures. No one can practise medicine in Canada without a licence. There already are penalties in the Criminal Code.
The Minister of Justice was quoted in The Globe and Mail on November 4 as saying that a deliberate decision was made to legislate by an amendment to the Criminal Code. Only by using the criminal law power can the federal government ensure a national approach to the question of abortion.
This bill does not provide a national approach to the issue. It allows provinces to pass restrictive laws to block access to abortion services just as we now see happening in the province of Nova Scotia. It does not set a national standard for accessibility.
The federal government sets standards for accessibility for other medical procedures through the Canada Health Act. The Minister of Justice cannot get away with saying that accessibility to health services is not a federal matter. The Canada Health Act is a federal statute that guarantees accessibility to medical services under threat of partial or complete withdrawal of federal funding for health care to the provinces. The Canada Health Act has already been used to guarantee that Canadians across this country could not be extra billed. The only national standard that this bill sets is the threat of criminal charges being brought against Canadian doctors for performing an abortion.
In the province of Prince Edward Island no abortion has been legally performed since 1982. Women from that province must go to Nova Scotia or another province to obtain an abortion. The Morgentaler clinic in Montreal has served women from as far away as Newfoundland. In Newfoundland there is only one doctor who is willing and allowed by a hospital board to perform abortions. When this doctor is ill or away on vacation no safe medical abortions are available in the province of Newfoundland.
Access to clinics in cities are physically blocked by protesters who harass women in an attempt to intimidate them. Women who have made probably the most difficult and the most agonizing personal decision of their lives are the targets of verbal abuse.
Those who say that there is already abortion on demand in Canada or that this law stands for something called abortion on demand are ignorant of the lengths that many Canadian women must go to to obtain an

November 7, 1989
Government Orders
abortion in this country. Even in provinces where access to abortion services are a lesser problem, we still see women forced to go to the United States. Not every woman in Canada lives in Toronto, Vancouver, or Montreal. Rural women have a very difficult time finding access to abortion services. If the doctor closest to them refuses, the woman must search further and further until she finds a doctor who will.
There is a serious problem of access in Canada, a problem this government has chosen to intensify rather than to address. Under this new law, women will have to shop around for a doctor who will brave the threat of criminal sanctions. At this point some doctors do not seem to believe that they will be charged for performing such a medical service because it really does seem to be an unbelievable thing that they could be. But we have seen under the old abortion law that several doctors were criminally charged for performing abortions. We have already heard the threats of the anti-choice extremists to charge doctors under this new law. The threat of being charged may keep some doctors from performing abortions, and access to a very needed health service may, in fact, be diminished.
This bill, if passed into law, will open the floodgate to a series of third party interventions. Disgruntled ex-boyfriends may lay an information that would bring criminal charges against doctors, and an aiding and abetting charge against women; anti-choice hospital personnel could charge doctors. There is no end to the legal lengths a certain faction of the anti-choice movement will go.
In the United States, a woman who was terminally ill and pregnant, decided, along with her husband and with her doctor, to wait a further two weeks before undergoing a Caesarean section because she knew and her doctor knew that the foetus would have a better change of survival at a more advanced gestational age. A third party court intervention led a judge to order an immediate Caesarean section against this woman's will. The foetus died within two hours and the woman died two days later. Third party interventions rob women of their dignity and of the right to make a decision about their own future. This is based on religious and philosophical principles that most of the population here in Canada do not share. We must not hand a new legal tool to this
extreme faction of the anti-choice movement. We cannot stand idly by and let what is currently happening in the United States happen here in Canada.
I am concerned about the criminal aspect of the bill and its implications for third party interventions and access. I add to that my disagreement with the conditions that it imposes on women.
I have three children, and giving birth was a joyous experience for me. It has been my most fulfilling life experience. But I was fortunate. I have a supportive husband. We were ready and prepared to have children. We were able to provide for their care. It was my choice to become a mother. I know what pregnancy is, and I know what childbirth is. It is not easy, and it is not simple. It is simply not inconvenient as some MPs in this House would suggest.
Some women choose not to bear children. A woman who makes this decision is not frivolous. To say this negates the value of motherhood. Motherhood is not to be taken lightly. It is not to be entered into by mistake or by force. Motherhood is a serious responsibility. Women who choose not to undertake it are not frivolous. Women are people of integrity. Women make careful and thoughtful decisions based on their own personal circumstances that we here do not have the right or the ability to prejudge.
Many women each year still die in childbirth. The question is not whether the doctor alone believes the woman's health is likely to suffer because of a pregnancy, it must be the woman's choice whether or not she decides that she should have a child.
The Minister of Justice has been using the language of choice when discussing this bill. There is no choice for women involved in this bill. The minister is being hypocritical when he uses the language of choice in relation to this bill which makes abortion the doctor's decision based on health criteria, not the women's choice based on her own personal criteria.
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Brian Dickson, said in the 1988 Morgentaler judgment, and I quote: "Forcing a woman by threat of criminal sanction to carry a foetus to term unless she meets certain criteria unrelated to her own priorities and aspirations is a profound interference with a woman's

body and thus a violation of security of the person". Chief Justice Dickson was not talking about meeting the state's health criteria to have an abortion. He did not say the woman should have to be measured against some standard that largely male politicians here will set up in order to have an abortion.
Madam Justice Bertha Wilson said that liberty in a free and democratic society does not require the state to approve the personal decisions made by its citizens. It does, however, require the state to respect them. The question then becomes whether the decision of a woman to terminate her pregnancy falls within this class of protected decisions. I have no doubt that it does. This decision is one that will have profound psychological, economic and social consequences for the pregnant woman. The circumstances giving rise to it can be complex and varied and there may be, and usually are, powerful considerations militating in opposite directions. It is a decision that deeply reflects the way the woman thinks about herself and her relationship to others and to society at large. It is not just a medical decision. It is a profound social and ethical one as well. The response to it will be the response of the whole person.
I would have hoped that in drafting this bill the conservative cabinet would have given more serious consideration to these words of wisdom. I believe if they had there would be no such bills in front of us today.
How far is this government going to take legislating state controls over a woman's body and personal decisions? What other aspects of women's personal lives are going to be left up to the state, the courts, and the medical profession to decide?
Canadians have varying moral, philosophical and religious beliefs about abortion. There is no reason for the state to impose what is, in fact, a minority moral belief about the equal status of the embryo or foetus upon all Canadian women. It is their own moral decision to make.
The church and the state are separate entities in modern Canadian society. They must remain separate. In Ireland and Brazil abortion is illegal, yet these two countries have a much higher abortion rate than we do here in Canada where abortion, prior to the passing of this bill, is still legal. The Minister of Justice said that this bill was not designed to reduce abortions. I do not understand this government. I do not understand why
Government Orders
any government would put a health service in the Criminal Code.
This bill does not reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies. It does not improve access for women across Canada. What is this bill meant to accomplish? What is it meant to do? There seems to be only one answer to that question. It seems that it is meant to quell the call for federal action on abortion. This government will now be able to say that it has dealt with the difficult issue of abortion.
What we should all be working for is to reduce the number of unwanted pregnancies in Canada. Bringing in restrictive legislation does not do this. Many people imagine that every sexually active person is completely knowledgeable about various methods of contraception, their effectiveness and the risks. Nothing could be further from the truth.
A 1987 Gallup poll showed that only 46 per cent of Canadians felt that they had adequate access to family planning information services. There was a great regional disparity in these findings, with only one-third of Atlantic Canadians reporting sufficient access to these services and to this information. Young people are at great risk of having misinformation about effective birth control and the risks of pregnancy. One 1986 Canadian study of teenagers has shown that only about one-half of sexually active teenagers always use contraception. The 1986 research discusses how one in six women in Ontario will become pregnant before she reaches the age of 20.
Only half the schools in Canada offered sex education in 1984. A 1982 study showed that only 57 per cent of medical doctors were prepared to provide teenagers with birth control resources. Planned Parenthood states that many parents do not feel prepared to provide thorough sexuality education for their children. Research indicates that the provision of reproductive health services and sex education reduce the number of teenage pregnancies.
According to a 1984 Gallup poll, 83 per cent of Canadians do support sex education in our schools, and half say the current level of school sex education is not adequate. Teenage women are not physically or emotionally prepared for pregnancy. Teenage mothers and their children experience a higher rate of mortality and of morbidity. It is cruel to deal with unwanted pregnancies simply by wrenching new born babies away from these

Government Orders
young women. The key, clearly, is prevention. Not enough is being done in this area.
In 1977 the family planning division at Health and Welfare Canada was disbanded. There is now only one full-time staff person in that huge department to work on family planning issues. Funding to Planned Parenthood was cut by $61,000 during this government's first mandate. In 1984, Planned Parenthood received $200,000 from the federal government, down from $447,000 in 1979. By 1988, Planned Parenthood was receiving only $139,000, a decrease of $61,000, not even taking inflation into account.
I questioned the Minister of National Health and Welfare about this in the House yesterday and he replied that Planned Parenthood funding had been increased for 1989 to $146,000. I am no mathematician, Mr. Speaker, and obviously the minister is not either, because this still represents a substantial long-term decrease in funding to Planned Parenthood of $54,000.
First the Liberals axed family planning, and then the Tories axed it, so that there is now an inadequate sum to address the desperate need for family planning education in this country. If this government were at all imaginative and serious about preventing unwanted pregnancies, it would consider the establishment of mobile family planning units that would visit schools and communities to disseminate birth control and sexuality information.
It could expand the role that Health and Welfare Canada plays in family planning education. This government could consider placing family planning ads on our television networks. Why in all of this discussion about recriminalizing abortion do we not hear one meaningful word from the government on family planning education?
Why is this government bringing in a restrictive criminal bill on abortion and not doing a single thing to reduce the numbers of unwanted pregnancies? Why cannot the government understand that the humane and the compassionate way to deal with the abortion issue is through progressive policies such as family planning education and not through punitive criminal legislation?
Another issue closely related to family planning education is research into the safe and effective means of contraception. The effectiveness of commonly available contraceptive devices leaves much to be desired.
A Canadian study of women experiencing unwanted pregnancies has shown that a full 64 per cent were using some form of birth control when they became pregnant. Part of the problem is a lack of knowledge about effective birth control. Many of the methods being used were not as effective as others such as condoms alone or the rhythm method.
Some 15 per cent were on the pill when they became pregnant. Although this is one of the most highly effective methods available, it is not 100 per cent effective for the typical user. The two most reliable forms of contraception, the birth control pill and sterilization, are also among those that pose the most health risks or that require a commitment to permanent infertility. Sterilization is obviously not an option for most teenagers or for any young man or young woman who is planning to have a family in the later stage of their life.
Celibacy has been touted as an answer to unwanted pregnancy. To think that married couples will not have sexual intercourse unless they are completely prepared to bring a child into this world is really preposterous. To think that teenagers inundated with sexual messages from the media will suddenly take to perhaps a decade of celibacy is also naive.
Sexuality is a part of the human existence. It is neither realistic nor healthy to try to force asexuality on adults and teenagers unless they are prepared to have children. Rather, the answer lies in effective contraception, safe contraception, and the services and education that will allow all sexually active people to avail themselves of these.
This government should make the funding into research of safe, effective contraception for men and women a priority. Along with failed birth control and inadequate information about birth control is the matter of women who want to have children but are held back because of social and economic factors. I have heard here and around these halls that socio-economic factors are not a reason to have an abortion. Now the government wants to entrench this dubious principle into criminal law.
November 7, 1989

Instead of outlawing these reasons why do we not work to eliminate them? Why expect women to plunge their families into poverty by having more children? Why not try to prevent the unwanted pregnancies and to eliminate the socio-economic conditions that lead women to forgo pregnancy that may very well otherwise be wanted?
According to the National Council on Welfare, almost one in five Canadian children is living below the poverty line today. The government proposes no action on this other than to force poor women to bear more children. One frequent result of poverty during pregnancy is low birth weight, which often leads to further medical complications.
According to the Quebec Corporation of Physicians babies born in certain Montreal and Quebec City neighbourhoods are as likely to be underweight at birth as those in underdeveloped countries. A recent Canadian study indicates that the child mortality rate is twice as high among families at the lowest income level than among those at the highest.
An Ontario study found that being on welfare is one of the strongest predictors of chronic health problems among children. Children are the largest group of users of food banks. A Calgary study of 132 public schools found that 46 reported significant problems with children coming to school hungry. Nutrition has led to success in school. Poor nutrition may lead to an inability to concentrate and poor vision.
Almost two-thirds of single parent families headed by women are living below the poverty line. A Planned Parenthood document states that for many women early parenting leads to poverty, poor health, a breakdown of current or future marriages and a lower level of formal education. It is hypocritical of the government to bring in a bill that criminalizes abortion for socio-economic reasons while the same government contributes to adverse socio-economic conditions for women through regressive economic policies.
The poverty rate for two parent families headed by a person under age 25 was 30 per cent in 1986. Two parents do not guarantee that a child will not grow up in poverty. The Canadian Council on Social Development states that even if both spouses were employed at the minimum they could earn only 92 per cent of the poverty line
Government Orders
income in 1986. Currently the federal minimum wage of $4 an hour is the lowest in Canada.
Poverty is a serious problem in Canada. Raising a child exacerbates the poverty a family may be experiencing or may contribute to poverty. We need to build a society in which children do not mean poverty to a woman or a family, a world in which children are not poor or hungry. The federal government can do much in the area of removing the economic barriers women face when considering whether or not to have a child, but this government seems to simply refuse to focus on economic strategies, on full employment, and adequate service. Instead it offers women regressive taxation and cutbacks. It has no compassion for the poor. This government's actions have been appalling.
It is the height of hypocrisy to make abortion for socio-economic reasons a crime and yet do nothing to eliminate the economic reasons why women feel that they have no other choice but an abortion in some instances. In fact, this government has exacerbated the problem of poverty in Canada by costing people their jobs with the trade deal and tossing thousands of people on welfare through its cut-backs to unemployment insurance and its taxation of the poor and the homeless with the new goods and services tax.
There are many things that this government has the power to do for women and especially for mothers. It could reindex and raise the family allowance. Instead it has dealt motherhood a blow by deindexing it and now it is clawing it back.
This government could expand the Canada Student Loans Program and the Canadian Jobs Strategy, making them more flexible and accessible for parents and young people. These are initial expenses that pay for themselves in the long run with a skilled workforce and a healthier economy. Language training and literacy should be a component of CJS. This would give many young women with small children a second chance to get the kind of education and employment that will allow them to feed their families.
The government could raise the minimum wage. How does the government expect women earning $4 an hour to be able to raise children? The government could also implement mandatory pay equity, employment equity

November 7, 1989
Government Orders
with goals and with timetables, rather than let women be economically penalized simply because they are women.
In our society women still bear the brunt of child rearing. Whether she has a spouse or not, a woman is usually expected to fulfil the demanding task of caring for and raising our children. Through inadequate or non-existing child support payments, women are often the only financial support as well as emotional and moral support of their families.
Women need to know that if they have a child they will not have to give up their job and livelihood, will not have to plunge themselves and their families into poverty, and that there is a support system in place which recognizes that many workers are also parents. In a 1988 survey
21,000	Canadian women said they were not paid labour force participants because they could not find subsidized child care. This government's policies are keeping women at home and keeping women in poverty.
The government came up with an inadequate strategy to deal with the ongoing child care crisis and then it abandoned even that. This government has shown no commitment to the children of Canada. Instead of recriminalizing abortion it should improve the situation for children and for parents in Canada. Instead of making hypocritical promises during the election campaign and breaking them after the election, this government should take positive action.
Canada's system of parental leave lags far behind that of most European countries. A pregnant woman in Canada must be employed in a UI insurable job between 10 and 20 weeks, depending on the regional rate of unemployment, to qualify for only 15 weeks of maternity leave with benefits equalling a maximum of 60 per cent of her insurable earnings.
A man or woman who is a new natural or adoptive parent and has met the qualifying criteria may take a 10-week parental leave at a maximum of 60 per cent of their insurable earnings to care for the infant, providing that the parent lives in a province or works for an employer who allows for this length of parental leave. The government cut parental leave for adoptive parents by five weeks this year. At the same time as the Conservatives are recriminalizing abortion, they are making it more difficult for adoptions to go through. This
is yet another example of the hypocrisy. There is usually a specified time that an adoptive parent must commit to stay at home with their new child. The government is imposing a financial burden on adoptive parents which may deter the adoption process.
Why does the government not expand parental leave to at least 24 weeks as a short-term goal with a view to further expansion and negotiate with the provinces to amend their labour codes to allow for parental leave?
We must also look into other ways in which workers with family responsibilities can be accommodated. We must take effective steps to make Canada a place in which children are welcome, in which children are an important and treasured part of our society. We cannot continue to carry on this government's course of ignoring children's needs: food, shelter and child care. Parents should be able to spend the time they need with their children without depriving themselves or depriving then-families. It has become so expensive to live that if a child has two parents usually both of them must work outside the home. Employers and government must recognize that workers have families and the economy must be restructured to take this fact into account.
Our social system requires women to be the primary care givers of children yet provides almost no support for pregnant women and new mothers. Women at a family life conference spoke of the inability of a blind mother of four to receive homemaker services. Support services must be accessible to all women. Support services pay for themselves in terms of healthy families and well adjusted individuals.
Sexually transmitted diseases may lead to infertility, birth defects, or even death. Health and Welfare Canada estimates that the cost of treating STDs in 1983 was $220 million. The direct cost of treating AIDS in 1985 was an estimated $192.6 million. This does not take into account the personal and social costs of these diseases. Half of all ectopic pregnancies which require emergency surgery to remove a fertilized ovum which is lost in a Fallopian tube is the result of a sexually transmitted disease. A government claiming to care about both foetuses and women should surely tiy to prevent STDs through education and accessible services. Governments should be involved in health protection and promotion, not in restricting reproductive choice for women.
November 7, 1989

The April 1989 federal budget cut $2 million from the Secretary of State women's program. Many of the groups funded through the program were involved in sharing information about issues, particularly issues affecting women including reproductive health. These groups have had their funding chopped by 15 per cent. The federal government cannot continue to evade its responsibilities in the area of health by claiming that it is a provincial matter. If health is only a provincial matter, why do we have a federal health statute guaranteeing accessibility and comprehensiveness among other things? That is what the Canada Health Act does.
If health is only a provincial concern, why does the federal government maintain a funding lever where health care provision is concerned? If health is a provincial matter, why do we have a federal Department of National Health and Welfare with a health promotion branch? The federal government should enforce the standards in the Canada Health Act to ensure access to adequate services which promote reproductive health and choice for all Canadians.
The abortion issue has centred around the ethics of abortion itself. What really needs to be discussed, however, is the ethics of a government that is prepared to restrict access to abortion but not prepared in any real way to address the reasons abortion takes place. The government's policies lead to economic hardship, inadequate planning, education and services, and environmental reproductive hazards. This government has shown concern for women and children. It is a government that sees abortion as a political issue, not a human issue, and is unwilling to look at ways to prevent unwanted pregnancies.
Prevention and support are the keys to creating real choices for women. Restricting abortion limits choice without addressing any of the reasons abortions occur. This abortion bill would reduce access to abortion, not reduce the numbers of unwanted pregnancies and abortions. It makes it more difficult to obtain an abortion, but it does nothing in the area of prevention. This bill also sets a precedent for handling unwanted pregnancies through criminal sanction rather than positive action. To me this bill says that women are not to be trusted. It says
Government Orders
that women are not people of integrity, that they cannot be trusted to make their own decisions around their own personal lives for themselves.
The abortion bill does one more thing. It shows Canadians this government's hypocrisy around this issue. This bill does not ensure equal access for the women in all regions of Canada-the women in Prince Edward Island, the women in the north, the women in the rural areas of my home province of British Columbia, or the women in the Atlantic provinces and Newfoundland.
It does nothing to improve access for these women. They must still travel to large urban centres like Montreal. They must pay the expenses of getting there. What does this say to women in Canada who are poor, who cannot afford to travel? What is the option for them when there is no access to abortion services in their own area? It does not work toward reducing the number of unwanted pregnancies. Criminalization will not prevent unwanted pregnancies. It does not make Canada a supportive society for women and children.
This issue is the fundamental emancipation and equality issue for the women of this country. This is the issue that the women of Canada look toward, whether or not they have ever considered for themselves the option of abortion, whether or not they have ever considered yet for themselves in their lives whether or not to have children. They view this issue as the fundamental issue that states that they are equal people in our society.
Hear, hear!

I urge members on both sides of this House: "speak to your mothers, speak to your sisters, speak to your daughters, speak to your wives. They understand this issue. They know. We know. Women know. We are people who can be trusted". I urge people on both sides of the House to vote in opposition to this bill for all women in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my voice today in a debate which over the course of the past year has bitterly divided citizens' groups, medical associations, the judiciary and Parliament itself. It has been a fierce and an emotional argument, an argument which has displayed the lives and experiences of individual Canadians across the front pages of newspapers and on the screens of millions of television sets throughout the country.
In the search for a solution to the abortion question, the public spotlight has sacrificed the privacy of everyone caught in the way, dissecting their experiences, emotions and entitlements. The rationale was that we were searching for a kernel of truth that would indicate clearly what was right and what was wrong. That is not the way in which an issue of this importance should be resolved. Sensationalizing individual lives cannot possibly provide the thoughtfulness, wisdom and judgment necessary to develop a bill which respects the rights of all Canadians, especially when those rights come into conflict with one another.

These rights relate to some very intimate matters. It is embarrassing for the people concerned and offensive for the rest of us to see these lives paraded in public. These are not issues that should be judged in a media trial.
It is not strictly a matter for the courts, either. However, there is ample evidence that in the absence of any initiative by Parliament, people will keep taking these matters before the courts.
Of course this kind of situation is unacceptable. It is not up to the courts to set policy, since the courts are not accountable to Canadians at election time. Clearly, it is up to our elected representatives to lead the way in this respect.
It is a role we have a duty to fulfil.

Many Canadians have very strong beliefs about whether abortion is right or wrong. In an issue which is so close to the hearts of each of us, we should not be surprised that some feel that it is their moral imperative to declare their stance as the only acceptable perspective in a caring world. When beliefs are held this deeply, they say there can be no concession.
I believe that we must search for common ground. Compromise is very difficult when groups cannot even agree to use the same vocabulary. When we politicize language itself we take away its meaning. Words no longer serve as tools to build understanding. They become weapons to discredit the views of others.
People who call themselves pro-choice in no way consider themselves to be anti-life. They feel that a woman's fundamental right to choose has been denied. It must now, when the right of women to determine their own futures is finally being recognized, be affirmed. And those who say they are pro-life flatly reject any claim that they are anti-choice. On the contrary, their entire effort has been to support the rights of those who cannot make their choices known because they do not yet have a voice.
We should not be surprised that the proposed legislation has not been endorsed by either pro-choice or pro-life groups because it does not use either's vocabulary.
There are few if any moral issues on which a consensus can be reached. However, the abortion isssue is stressful for each and everyone of us because it seems to call for a decision that negates one essential human value while benefiting another.
November 7, 1989

Government Orders
We should not be surprised at the intensity and bitterness of this debate. The fact that democracy encourages protest in our search for the truth is one of its strong points. However, it does not encourage protest for protest's sake. It tends to promote debate and argument so that we can finally agree on what is best for society.

We have been elected by Canadians to choose the course which best balances the rights of everyone concerned. We do not seek to disguise the fact that the bill is a compromise. It is a proposal which accepts the validity of opposing points of view. It recognizes that while abortion must always be a last resort, probably there will always be instances where it is necessary. Each case must be considered separately. We have provided room for that consideration in this legislation.
Over the years my position has been pro-life. I cannot pretend that each word of this legislation is exactly what I would have written in an ideal world, but I do believe that if we want legislation at all, we must compromise. Building on compromise, we must show tolerance. We must try to understand opinions which are different from our own. I do not mean that we have to agree completely, but rather that more than one opinion must be reflected in the law.
Society's values change with time and our laws change with them. The one constant must be our respect for one another. The social contract which guides our conduct with one another is not based on a principle of winner take all.
Twenty-two months ago the Supreme Court, interpreting the Charter of Rights, struck down the previous law on abortion. It recognized that society must choose among competing rights. But the country was left without a framework for making that choice.
The government on Friday, after much soul searching and compromise, tabled this bill. Some people have already declared their opposition. But what is their alternative, to have no law, as we have had for the last 22 months; to leave a policy vacuum, where depending on your point of view, everything or nothing is acceptable?

Obviously, we have a duty to specify the kind of context in which women and their doctors can make such sensitive decisions. The bill before the House today represents the best attempt at a compromise we have seen so far.
We have looked at other options. Some people felt that we could use the provisions of the Canada Health Act.

We have been asked to use the Canada Health Act in two ways. On the one hand, there are advocates of abortion rights who are concerned about the availability of abortion services. They would like us to financially penalize those provinces which do not provide unrestricted services.
The leader of the NDP argued for that approach yesterday. He made the case for invoking the Canada Health Act on abortion, but was not prepared to argue that the federal government should attempt to dictate how services that may be crucial to the very survival of patients, such as neurosurgery, cancer treatment, or heart surgery, should be delivered. Abortion would apparently be the only case where such a weapon would be used.
On the other hand, the pro-life groups have stated that the federal government should use the Canada Health Act to deny payments to provinces which provide abortion services.
Neither of these two alternatives is consistent with current constitutional practice in Canada. The provision of health services is primarily a matter of provincial jurisdiction. According to the Constitution, the provinces are responsible for the operation and delivery of the health care services which all Canadians cherish.
That fact was recognized when Parliament legislated on this issue in 1969. The then Minister of Justice who is today the Leader of the Opposition, described the role of the provinces clearly. He said this:
The relationships in civil law between the patient and the doctor, between the patient and the nurse, between the doctor and the hospital, the nurse and the hospital, are relationships falling within the operation of provincial law, the civil law, and the constitutional responsibility of the provinces -the subject of statutes which regulate hospitals and professions. These are properly provincial matters.

November 7, 1989
Government Orders

The Canada Health Act respects provincial jurisdiction in health matters and recognizes the fact that our provincial health systems have evolved in ways that are characteristic of each province.
The Act's criteria provide general guidelines, deliberately leaving the provinces with a certain latitude in deciding how they are to be applied, so that they can make decisions based on local priorities and capabilities.

If you read the Canada Health Act, Mr. Speaker, you will find that it does not list specific medical services, whether they be cancer treatment, heart surgery or abortion services. The provinces, in conjunction with the medical profession, are responsible for deciding what is medically necessary. The provinces licence medical practitioners and regulate medical institutions such as hospitals. They also decide how best to organize the service and provide access.
The bottom line is that the federal government cannot dictate policies in areas of provincial jurisdiction. It would be an invasion of the provinces' role in Confederation. As the House will know, the constitutionality of the Canada Health Act is currently being challenged. We believe that the act will survive, however, because it respects provincial jurisdiction as it is currently written.
It is only through the criminal power that Parliament can regulate abortion on a national basis. The proposed legislation will give the provinces the guidance they have requested on the legal framework for abortion.
I expect that with the provision of this new legal framework, provincial governments will respect both the letter and the spirit of the law and will arrange for access to all medically necessary services. The federal government will encourage consistency in their responses, recognizing varying provincial circumstances.
Some people have proposed a gestationally based alternative which would divide pregnancy into two or three stages, permitting abortion in the early period and limiting it near the end. The problem is, the boundary line between stages is very difficult to define and it changes with advances in technology. The notion of
foetal viability has evolved significantly in the last five years. Finally, the government's legislation, unlike a gestational approach, recognizes society's interest in the foetus right from the earliest stages.
That is the rationale for the the legislation before the House. We believe that it is moderate and reasonable and that it deserves the support of Canadians. But there are other issues that Parliament must also address. Each year, about 360,000 children are bom in Canada. About
65,000	abortions take place. Over half of them are performed on women under the age of 25. Our challenge is to put in place policies that support Canadian families and that eliminate the causes of such high numbers of abortions.
Most of the women who undergo these abortions know firsthand of the agonizing choice that is being made to prevent a baby from being bom. They do not take the decision lightly. They know that abortion must never be seen as just another form of birth control. Our priority must be to educate young people to be responsible and also to eliminate the economic, social and personal injustices which encourage such a choice.
In the past, policies have been ad hoc and have looked at these issues in isolation from each other. I believe it is time for our country to take a much more comprehensive approach to sexual health, family planning and how we raise our children. The goal must be to help Canadians make informed choices which will create strong and stable families.
One key element was put in place a few days ago when the Prime Minister announced the Royal Commission on New Reproductive Technologies. Too many Canadian families would like to have children but cannot. The royal commission has been asked to study the causes, treatment and prevention of male and female infertility, reversals of sterilization and a host of other reproductive health issues.
We want Canadians to have the widest possible range of options in deciding whether and when they will have children.

We are also taking steps to help families that already have children. We want to fight family violence and child

sexual abuse. We want to improve daycare services and help Canadian families get out of the poverty trap.
We are taking these steps to make the family a healthy environment for the child and to correct certain situations that make women consider abortion as a last resort.
We also have to look for more effective ways to help women avoid unwanted pregnancies and to cope with these pregnancies when they occur.
In 1977 the federal government of the day agreed with the provinces that the provision of birth control services is primarily a provincial responsibility. Services which were previously delivered by the Family Planning Division of the Department of National Health and Welfare would in the future be provided by them. However, there is a key role which is left for the federal government to play in sponsoring research and providing financial assistance to national organizations involved in the field.
I have asked that the Department of National Health and Welfare earmark a minimum of $500,000 a year over the next three years for research into family planning issues, including contraception and problems in fertility. We also need better information and education. Recognizing that the nature of the problem changes from community to community, we will continue to give sustaining grants to two national organizations, Planned Parenthood of Canada and Serena Canada, to educate, promote and support family planning which is sensitive to the varying needs of different communities.
Another way to reduce the number of abortions performed in this country is to encourage more adoptions. There are thousands of would-be parents who are unable to have their own children and would provide loving homes. We need to encourage more pregnant women to consider adoption as an alternative.
As a result, the federal government plans to sponsor and fund a study to identify factors that could make adoption more appealing to young single mothers. I plan shortly to issue a call for proposals to conduct this study. I hope that it will point to solutions that place more
Government Orders
babies into the homes of Canadians who are otherwise unable to fulfil their aspirations to be caring parents.
Through our health promotion contributions program, we will continue to fund proposals for community-based projects which will help adolescents lead responsible reproductive lives.

A lack of accessible and affordable resources to deal with matters concerning health, reproduction and sexuality has been obvious for some time. Although community organizations, local agencies and provincial departments continue to create new facilities and purchase new equipment, the lack of co-ordination and communication between agencies often leads to duplication and unnecessary spending.

In my opinion, we have an urgent need for balanced and clearly explained information on human sexuality. As a result, we are giving Planned Parenthood Federation of Canada $264,000 toward the development of a national resource centre on reproductive health and human sexuality to provide that information co-ordination.
As I mentioned earlier, each year there are about
360,000	pregnancies brought to term in Canada. But not all the mothers and fathers have the resources which they need to help them develop their knowledge and skills to be good parents. We are in the process of launching two national programs designed to help new parents. The first, the post-partum parent support program, helps new mothers, their partners and other members of the family cope with the arrival of a new child. The second is aimed at the 150,000 young, single, low-income parents we have in Canada, many of whom feel isolated from support and some of whom lack confidence in their ability to raise a child well. This program, which we are undertaking in co-operation with the provinces, will give parents accurate information on their children's health, safety, development and behaviour. We hope to prevent further unplanned pregnancies by making sure people understand the choices open to them in choosing whether to have children.
In an age characterized by the spread of the AIDS and other sexually transmitted diseases, over-population, child abuse and unwanted pregnancy, we must educate

November 7, 1989
Government Orders
ourselves, provide better and more accessible birth control information and methods and revolutionize the way in which we approach the sexual education of our young.
The issue of abortion cuts to the root of deeply held moral conviction about the meaning of human life and the control of life and death by the instruments of modem technology. As yet, no consensus exists in North America on these issues.
It is tempting on such questions to refuse to consider any significant compromise. That is the position taken by the spokespersons for some organized groups well before they ever saw the bill. Members have that option and some have already said that they will exercise it. Their actions will be applauded by the groups which reject any compromise. To follow that course, however, is to leave without a voice the majority of Canadians who do not belong to such groups and who expect this Parliament to show leadership in building a consensus.
They believe that Canadian women and their doctors have the right to know when abortions may be performed and when they may not. They believe that the private lives of Canadians should not be fought out the media and in the courts. Most important, they believe that it is our responsibility as elected representatives to set the policy, not to leave it to the judges to set by default.
The bill before us today represents a moderate and balanced compromise to an ethical conundrum. Its alternative is stalemate and a legal vacuum. I urge members to consider this legislation carefully, to accept our responsibility to provide the leadership which Canadians are demanding and to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I applaud the list of efforts the federal government is planning for the support of women and wonder when we will begin to see them coming into actual fact. The minister can rest assured that we will be watching to ensure that they do become fact and are not just another empty announcement.
The Minister of Finance, during the speech delivered by my colleague, the hon. member from New Westminster-Burnaby, said in a heckle that only the NDP would bring free trade into the abortion issue. That to me suggests that the hon. member still fails to understand that abortion and the attendant control over women and
their bodies is an economic issue that has been inflamed throughout history in order to maintain economic control over women.
The minister referred to my leader's request that access to abortion be regulated by the Canada Health Act. He said that neurosurgery, heart and cancer treatment is not regulated under the Canada Health Act, and so suggested that access to abortion should not be as well.
I would suggest that neurosurgery, heart and cancer treatment is denied because of lack of facilities, not because of someone's moral opinion. I would suggest also that if a whole province refused to do or pay for heart surgery, then the minister and his government would have much to say under the Canada Health Act about that.
I would appreciate it very much if the minister would respond to this question. If a province refused to pay for or facilitate heart surgery, would he, under the Canada Health Act, intervene?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would first of all make one minor correction to the reference to me that was made by the hon. member when she referred to me as the Minister of Finance. I have been here now some 17 years and the great achievement of my political career will be if I can spend my whole career here without ever becoming Minister of Finance. I am sure the Minister of Finance would agree that it would be in the public interest that that be avoided as well.
The hon. member tries to argue again, as her leader did yesterday, that the federal government should refuse to fund medicare services provided in the provinces if they refuse to provide the level of service for abortion which the hon. member would like to see. She does not indicate whether she believes the federal government should be dictating, in the case of these other services she mentioned such as cancer treatment where the very survival of the patient depends upon it, that that treatment should be provided or that it should be provided in a particular way. She does not indicate, in the case of neurosurgery or in the case of heart disease or a whole range of other areas, that the federal government should intervene to require that these services be provided. Look at an issue, for example, related to reproduction. A
November 7, 1989

number of the provinces right now are looking at the question of midwifery. It is an area which is left to provincial jurisdiction. Would the hon. member argue that the federal government should set one policy which would apply from one coast to another which would give women the choice of whether or not they wanted to go to a midwife to deliver a child? No, she says, she would not want to do that.
Indeed, what the NDP is asking for is that any medical services which are provided by provinces, the sole instance in which they ask for federal intervention with us using a financial weapon against the provinces is to require the provinces to increase services on abortion; not in any other instances, they say, solely in the case of abortion. Such an approach would be unconstitutional.
I would invite the hon. member to read the Canada Health Act and she will recognize the fact if she does that the Canada Health Act was deliberately designed by the government of the day, which was a Liberal government, voted on and supported by Parliament, by all of the parties, to ensure that the constitutional rights of all jurisdictions were respected.
Finally, she takes umbrage at the reference I made from this side of the House at the time the member for New Westminster-Burnaby was giving her oration when she tried to attribute the high rate of abortion in Canada to the free trade agreement. I repeat, only the NDP would attempt to so partisanize debate on abortion that they would drag the free trade agreement in and try to blame that for the high rate of abortion in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to the minister and his comments about the attempts that he said that his government was going to make with respect to education of the public. I wonder if the minister would be kind enough to help with the education of the public at the present time.
I would like to pose two questions. Precisely what is the purpose of banning abortion? What do I mean by that question? Surely we have to ask ourselves what is an abortion. That has to be the fundamental question asked of this House and it can only be after we have come to grips with that question and with the answer to it that we decide whether or not abortion should be allowed.
Government Orders
The government obviously has brought forward a bill which clearly makes abortion illegal in this countiy unless certain circumstances apply. I would like to know on what rationale that decision is based, and if in fact it is based on some rationale to protect foetal rights at some point, what foetal rights? Why do they need protection?
Of course, my position is clear and I will be making it abundantly clear when I speak on this bill, and that is that life begins at conception. I would just like to know how we can discuss the issue of abortion and banning abortion without talking about what abortion is and putting a definition.
My second question concerns subclause 3 of clause 287 as proposed, which deals with various drugs. I am asking the minister if he and his government have discussed whether or not that section would include such drugs as RU-486 which is presently being manufactured in France and whether or not that drug would be excluded under clause 3.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, any attempt to have that drug used in Canada would require that an application be made to the Department of National Health and Welfare for approval. The intention of the legislation was to ensure that such things as birth control devices, intrauterine devices, so-called morning-after pills, were permitted but not to allow other means of inducing abortion in Canada except as permitted by the law. No application has been made at the present time for such a pill to be marketed in Canada.
It is not our intention to ban abortion in Canada and I think that it is important, as we discuss this issue, to have an understanding of what this bill is designed to do. The goal is not to ban abortion but rather to set the framework in which decisions can be taken as to when abortion will be permitted in Canada.
One of the fundamental decisions that we take is that it is essentially a health matter to be decided between the woman and her doctor. We have made it clear that we do see competing rights here, that we believe the society does have an interest in the unborn child. But we believe as well that when the health of the mother is threatened, the woman in question and the doctor should have the right to have and perform an abortion in that instance. By setting this framework, we believe that we help to give a clear sense of direction to the women of Canada and also to the doctors in Canada as to when

November 7, 1989
Government Orders
abortion will be permitted and when it will not, and we attempt to balance these competing rights.
I think there probably is no one in this House who believes in the issue as foetal rights, as the hon. member does, who would not recognize the fact that what we are dealing with foetus versus the rights of the woman in question. The goal of this bill is to try to strike a balance between those rights and to give a clear indication as to when it is appropriate that abortion should be permitted in Canada.
Finally, I would welcome an indication from the hon. member as to whether he supports the position that was taken by his party spokesman earlier in favour of using the Canada Health Act to intervene against the provinces, to withhold money from the provinces if they do not expand abortion services in Canada. Was the hon. member who spoke earlier speaking on behalf of his party in that regard?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment of the House are as follows: the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Employment; the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre-Agriculture-Removal of oats from Canadian Wheat Board/Results of Decima poll; the hon. member for Beaver River-The Senate.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lewis that Bill C-43, an act respecting abortion, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, abortion is a complex issue, perhaps the most complex issue to be faced by this House in the current session or any other session of our long parliamentary history. It is fraught with emotional arguments on both sides and it is crucial that we respect the views of both sides in so far as they have an inalienable right to hold and express such views. It is an issue that must be faced and dealt with in our pluralistic society with both honesty and integrity. This bill is not the answer.
This bill gives the false impression that politicians are not honest, because this bill is not honest. On the one hand, it says abortion is prohibited throughout pregnancy. On the other, it creates a loophole which effectively allows for any and all abortions. Now, some will say, why argue? The actual effect of this bill once passed into law is that anyone who wants an abortion will get one.
The two proposed amendments to Section 287 and Section 288 of the Code make all abortions illegal in Canada, except in cases where a physician is of the opinion that the woman's physical, mental and, and I believe or, psychological health is endangered by the continuance of the pregnancy. In any other circumstance, it is a criminal offence punishable by up to two years imprisonment for anyone to induce an abortion, including self-inducement of an abortion by a female person. In addition, no person can lawfully supply or procure a drug or other noxious thing, or an instrument or thing, for the purposes of inducing an abortion, which again would include the pregnant woman in cases of self-inducement.
From a legal perspective, this bill would not survive a constitutional challenge, as far as I am concerned, in the Supreme Court, in light of the Morgantaler decision. It certainly does not respect Madam Justice Wilson's judgment on the right to "liberty of the person" to choose for herself what happens to her body. Nor does it respect the judgments of Justices Dickens, Lamer, Betz
November 7, 1989

with regard to the security of the person under Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
The right to security of the person includes a right of access to medical treatment and protection from significant delays in seeking medical treatment. Replacing the requirement of hospital committees to that of only one physician does not change the issue of access since there is absolutely no guarantee that all physicians in Canada would apply the same standard criteria in assessing the health of a pregnant person.
There is also no guarantee that a physician's moral and religious values will not dictate his or her assessment of the need for an abortion. There are no standards or guidelines for all of Canada's physicians to follow, except for, and I quote: "generally accepted standards of the medical profession". Whatever that may mean, they can and do differ from province to province and from territory to province.
As a result of such legislation women certainly do not have equal access before the law, and nor is the law applied equally to all as is required by Section 15.
The interesting thing is that the government had an opportunity to do something here. It is likely that the Supreme Court would accept legislation that would ban abortions after 22 weeks of pregnancy except for medical reasons dictated by the expectant mother's condition or that of the unborn child. Indeed, this has been recommended by both the Law Reform Commission of Canada and the Canadian Medical Association. But this is not what the government has given us. Anyone who wants one can get one. That I submit is not the effect of this bill, even if that is its intention.
The question of access, as we have seen, is not addressed. Indeed, it appears that because the bill is silent on access this crucial issue will be thrown back to the provinces and territories, creating 12 different scenarios at a minimum.
I think the thing that is perhaps the most abhorrent about this legislation is that to secure an abortion women in most cases will have to lie. They will have to fabricate a situation for their doctors to ensure that they fall within the definition of a threat to health; physical, mental, or psychological health. What does that mean?
Government Orders
What does it mean medically, and what does it mean practically?
This bill places the onus for the decision squarely with the doctors. Although the Minister of Justice this morning and the Minister of National Health and Welfare this afternoon, in discussing the bill both spoke of a decision between a woman and her doctor, the bill does not say that. The concept of consultation is intrinsic to the woman's right to choose. Clearly she can accept or reject a doctor's recommendation. No one is suggesting anything other than that. But to leave her out of the specifics of the legislation implies a denial of her right to be a full participant in that decision.
The legislation raises more questions. Does it meet the requirements of the security of the person delineated by Section 7 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms? Does it meet the minimum requirements relating to time again set down by the Morgentaler decision? What about women living in remote rural areas whose only access may be a doctor who, as would be his or her right, does not choose to perform abortions? The legislation does not even address this situation.
What about women who convince a doctor that their mental, psychological, or physical health will be impaired by bearing a child? In particular, if they insist that it is their mental or psychological health that is in danger, will this contention, true or false, entered into their permanent medical records come back to haunt them at some future date? The ramifications for the female population of the process may indeed be more detrimental to their health than pregnancy or abortion.
The vast majority of people find abortion abhorrent, and so it is. It goes against every human inclination to protect the helpless. But it is equally abhorrent to the majority of Canadians to force a woman to bear a child when she finds the situation untenable. Few people quarrel with abortion in the context of rape or incest, but there are other situations equally tragic for women; the mother who has neither the financial nor emotional resources to support another child, the teenager frightened out of countenance and unable to cope with the responsibility and equally unable to seek support from her family, the abused wife with nowhere to turn, the woman who does not see parenthood as an option, the woman who is responsible in her sexual life but whose

November 7, 1989
Government Orders
contraception failed. We do not live in rose-covered cottages.
We do not live in ideal situations and far, far too many Canadian women and their children live lives of quiet desperation. Some people just say "Well, that's tough. You made your bed, you must lie in it", or "You made your choice when you became sexually active". There is not much compassion there and there is not really very much common sense either.
If abortion is banned it will not cease. Personally, I am not excessively worried that women will resort to butchers because Canadian doctors are too compassionate to let that happen. But normally law-abiding women and equally law-abiding doctors will flout any flat ban by the thousands. Can anyone turn their back to the woman who faces an alcoholic husband who is demanding his so-called marital rights on the night he gets his pay cheque and say "You made your choice and you must live with it"?
These would be bad laws as this bill will be a bad law. This bill is a bad law because it tacitly invites women and doctors to bend the facts to fit the legislation. If the intent of the law is to ban abortion then the intent is thwarted. If the intent is to allow abortion then the government should say so. Women do not want their rights surreptitiously through the back door. Neither do those Canadians who hold the view that abortion is totally unacceptable deserve to be tricked into thinking, presupposing the trick worked, that this bill stops abortion. This bill is not balanced, it is not compromise. It is sham and Canadians recognize sham.
Since the abortion law was struck down last year, there has been no perceptible increase in abortions. Women do not make these decisions lightly. The agony that all fair-minded people go through in considering the rights of the woman vis-a-vis the rights of the foetus is small, compared to the agony faced by the vast majority of women when they decide they cannot continue their pregnancies. This is a private personal and tragic situation in which parliamentarians, interest groups and the media really should not be able to meddle because the answer, the solution, is not and never has been found in legislation, and certainly not in criminal legislation.
Yes, we have a collective responsibility to act and yes, there is a societal right here, but it is being obscured by the emotion of the debate. What we must act on are long-term solutions and the only real way to create real choice is to create the situation where child-bearing and child-rearing are freely chosen and widely supported, supported by concrete actions and not merely pious do-nothing lip service.
This bill does not even attempt to address the long term, but worst of all, there is no sign of any companion legislation to help to minimize the need for abortion, to create a real freedom of choice for women and men.
There are three basic ingredients to a long-term solution. The first is massive education, not small programs, a little bit here, a little bit there. As a society and a country we have never faced squarely the matters of sexuality and responsibility. We are a nation of ostriches, burying our heads in the sand in these days of fatal sexually-transmitted diseases and unwanted pregnancies. The just say no theory is weak to the point of irresponsibility. Federal and provincial governments must work together now to educate the population.
The Hon. Minister of Health espoused some of this idea in his speech. I say to him that women and children need more than words. Five hundred thousand dollars here and $264,000 there is a pittance, it is not enough. If we are going to put our money where our mouths allegedly are, it has to be substantial money that makes substantial change. The women and children of Canada do not need budget cuts and they certainly do not need the GST.
The second is the development of safe, adequate and affordable contraception. Again our society is remiss. We place the responsibility for contraception heavily on the female but provide methods that either seriously jeopardize a woman's health or have a failure rate that no odds-maker would depend on. Sadly, there is no move of any significance on the part of this government in this direction. Rather, we have seen cuts, cuts and more cuts.
The third is a concerted effort to make this country truly supportive of families, of mothers and of their children. What support is there for the pregnant 14-year-old scared out of her mind, for the abused wife, for the woman on welfare who cannot scrape together a decent living for her family, for the one million children
November 7, 1989

in Canada who live in poverty and must depend on food banks, for the physically abused child, for the emotionally abused child and for the sexually abused child?
What about the 70 per cent of child support orders in this country that go unenforced? Above all, what about child care? Where is the child care legislation that would provide not just support, but the intention of a new dawn in caring about families in this country?
If anyone thinks that these matters are unrelated to the abortion issue, then we have even more ostriches than we originally thought. If this were a perfect world- and my colleague the Minister of Justice said that earlier today-a world without violence and without fear, abortion would not be the issue it is today.
If this government were committed to achieving a better level of social justice, a decent standard of living and some alleviation of the plight of the poor, we would be on the road to solving this complex and terrible problem. Instead, we have a bill that insults the intelligence of both sides, that forces women to lie, that institutionalizes hypocrisy. It is just not good enough.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from the Liberal party for her comments today. She and I share the same critic responsibilities for our respective parties and it is a pleasure to be in the House together.
I have a couple of questions for the member. She is from a region of Canada where the access problem is veiy difficult and where women travel distances and have great difficulty in finding doctors or facilities that perform abortion. I wonder if she could comment on that and on some of the women in rural areas of Atlantic Canada who have great difficulty in accessing services for safe abortion.
Also, could she comment on what this does to women who do not have money, women who are poor? What do they do when they need access to a safe abortion? How do they get to the area of the country that will provide such a service?
My second question deals with her comments relating to the Law reform Commission and the issue of gestational limits. I have a fundamental belief that gestational limits indeed are wrong. From her comments I under-
Govemment Orders
stood that she might perhaps support the concept of the Law Reform Commission.
I have a friend who was five and one-half months pregnant this summer with a third child, very much a wanted child. My friend was diagnosed with a very aggressive form of cancer. She was told by her doctor that she must undergo an abortion in an attempt to save her life. I know how difficult this was for my friend because she shared this pain with me.
I am opposed to gestational limits because my friend and other women in situations like that would then be forced to go through another process or another board or another medical opinion. Would she just comment on the concept of gestational limits as well?

I thank my hon. colleague, the other critic for status of women. Indeed we do share many of the same views on this.
Just to comment on the gestational approach, we do not have legislation in front of us that reflects it, but I certainly find it to be possibly the legislation that might come closest to the compromise that many of us desire. In any legislation that reflected the gestational view, I would not see a situation such as the one of the woman five and a half months pregnant and needing an abortion due to a serious threat to life to be a drawback.
I do not think the Supreme Court would allow us to legislate a problem with time. That is already covered in Morgentaler. I think the gestational approach merely reflects what is the actual situation in medical practice in this country. Certainly the decision of a woman and her doctor at a later point would obviously reflect what is already medical practice in this country.
On the first question with regard to access, we note that in Alberta, for example, access, especially in the north, continues to be a problem. Access in Saskatchewan is very poor with the few centres which provide abortion restricting their services to local women. In Manitoba access is concentrated in Winnipeg. Many New Brunswick women, especially from the North Shore, must travel to the United States or Montreal to access an abortion.
In Nova Scotia over 80 per cent of the province's abortions are performed at one hospital in Halifax. In Prince Edward Island women must travel outside of P.E.I. to obtain abortions as no hospital there will perform them. In Newfoundland, St. John's General
