Hospital is the only one that provides abortions on a regular basis and access is dependent on a particular doctor at a particular time.
The answer is that poor women are in a worse bind. If I may, and I mean no levity at this whatsoever, in Atlantic Canada where the preferred means of travel of the poor is the train, we have another problem as well. Women who wish to come from northern New Brunswick and the rural areas of Nova Scotia have depended upon the train and that has been taken away from them, how or will be taken away from them. How they are going to afford to get to the regional centres where they can access an abortion, I do not know, but I do know that this bill does not help them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have a question. Given the context of the Charter of Rights and a mother going to a doctor requesting an abortion, does the member feel that the doctor, on a woman's request, is obligated to provide that abortion?

I said quite clearly that a doctor obviously has a right to preferred areas of practice. Some doctors will choose not to perform an abortion, and that is certainly the right of the individual doctor. But it is incumbent upon us, and indeed I believe that this House was certainly given a very broad hint by the Supreme Court of Canada, to look at improving access in a manner that we can control. I am not suggesting that I or the hon. member or a posse from the House of Commons should seek out doctors across the country and put guns to their heads and say "you will perform abortions". That is ridiculous. Access can be answered in manners other than that. Among other things, it can be answered through the Canada Health Act.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as you might detect, I was thinking that we would probably be dealing with this issue a little later. As a matter of fact, I had in mind speaking on this bill tomorrow but the opportunity presented itself this afternoon and I thought I would use it to speak on this bill in the House of Commons.
I see the member across the way, the Minister of Energy, the former minister of health. I must say that his present portfolio presents a little less of a problem to him than if he were the minister of health at this particular time. Having read this bill, I can tell that the
Minister of Energy certainly did not write it. I sympathize with the Minister of Energy and others who, like myself, want a bill which protects human life, as this bill does not. However, unlike the Minister of Energy, I am not constrained by the fact that I am a member of the cabinet and, therefore, will be able to vote in a manner which is more consistent with my conscience rather than a discipline which is imposed.
I do not say that in a light-hearted way or in any way to make fun of the position in which some of our colleagues find themselves as a result of being in cabinet. I suppose every member of this House wants to be in cabinet at some point, but I am sure there are moments like this when members of cabinet find that being there has its difficult moments as well. I make those comments for that reason. I do not want any member to think that my comments should be interpreted otherwise, particularly not when I speak on such a very important issue as this, and when I address some of the remarks to the Minister of Energy, whom I respect immensely for the position which I believe he has on this issue.
Mr. Speaker, as I said in July 1988, when I made my speech in the House of Commons, I have changed my mind on this issue, and I announced this change in my views in April 1988. I realized that for any politician, changing ones stand is not always very popular and is even quite controversial. Even more so if ones says so in public. And that is what I did at the time. I changed my mind on the abortion issue, simply because I could no longer live with the position I had taken, and when I say that, I am not referring to outside pressure but to pressure from within. In other words, my conscience would no longer let me live with the position I had taken at the time. Since April 1988, Mr. Speaker, I have tried to explain to my colleagues in this House and to any Canadians who cared to listen that the only bill that should be passed by this Parliament and this House should respect and protect life before and after birth.
In 1959, before the United Nations, Canada justified the importance of our participation in the Declaration of the Rights of the Child. At the time, Mr. Speaker, we as Canadians told the nations of the world that the child not yet born needed special protection, and that the handicapped child should be given special protection and care before and after birth. Today, in 1989, some people
November 7, 1989

say: If a child is going to be handicapped, that is grounds for having an abortion and preventing that child from being born. I keep wondering what happened to us in the last thirty years that made us give up all those values we had acquired since the age of Hippocrates and even before then-Hippocrates said that a doctor had no right to suggest or give medication that would result in the death of a patient, and he even said that one should never offer a woman a pessary to induce abortion. Since that time and even before then, since the time of Hippocrates, that great Greek physician, we as a society have taken the position that we should protect human life, the life of the child yet to be born and the life of any person. And now we are qualifying that position, when we say that if the child yet to be born will be handicapped, we should not allow it to live.
I think we have reached a sorry stage in the history of human civilization. Incidentally, this is not a typically Canadian problem. It is a problem the world over. I keep thinking that we are very regressive in the way we look at things, and I find this very sad.

The bill that we have before us today is deficient in a number of ways and I will spend the next few minutes expressing the amendments that I would like to see to this bill in order to make it acceptable.
First this bill states, in its first sentence, that abortion is wrong. In other words, "Every person who induces an abortion-is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to imprisonment". This, of course, makes the clear statement that abortion is a criminal offence and should be treated as a crime.
However, the bill is deficient as it goes along. First of all, we are discussing here a term of imprisonment not to exceed two years. I would submit to my colleagues in the House of Commons that if we are to consider abortion to be a crime, a term of two years does not reflect the fact that it is a crime. I believe that that penalty should be stricter and should reflect the seriousness of that statement.
Criminal law does two things; one, it punishes a guilty individual or an individual who behaves in a way unacceptable to society as a whole and, second, it makes a statement of where we stand in that society. It makes a
Government Orders
statement of what we think is right and what we think is wrong. If we are to consider abortion to be a crime, which this bill does, then surely the punishment should reflect that. That sentence of the bill continues:
-	unless the abortion is induced by or under the direction of a
medical practitioner-
I will speak in a few moments on when I think abortion should be permitted which, as some of my colleagues may have detected by now, is not very often. In any case, before we get to that point, I do not believe that an abortion should ever be induced, on the few occasions where they should be, by anyone other than a doctor. Where the sentence says "induced-under the direction of" I believe that an amendment would be necessary to the bill.
The other deficiency that I see in this bill is that the next sentence continues and says:
-a medical practitioner who is of the opinion that,-
It describes when the abortion should be performed. I think that bill should be amended to say, starting with the same sentence, "-unless the abortion is induced by a medical practitioner having received the opinion of two other medical practitioners stating that the abortion is necessary".
In other words, I do not believe that Henry Morgental-er should say: "Abortion is necessary for this woman and, by the way, I will do it right now." I do think that the medical practitioner should be giving an independent opinion. As a matter of fact, I think there should be two of them.
I want to read further because my time is close to ending. The sentence of the bill continues:
-	if the abortion were not induced, the health or life of the female
person would be likely to be threatened.
I think that that should be changed to say only: "the life of the female person would likely be threatened". The word "health" in the previous section of the Criminal Code was completely bent out of shape from its original meaning and we are inviting that by putting it in the bill this time again.
I would like to have commented quite a bit more about this bill. I hope to have the opportunity to offer some of the amendments which I think would go a long way toward making this bill a bill which will protect human life from the time of conception.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party as our party's communications and culture critic to present this very important motion to the House.
While this motion addresses the question of control or ownership of communications tools, it gives us in the House an opportunity to address the issue of foreign control over our culture and what we can do about it.
The issues of communications broadcasting, control of culture and our cultural independence are issues that will be among the key issues of the 1990s. They, the environment and other issues, will be the issues we will have to deal with in a decade because we are going to see change very rapidly. We are going to see new technologies. We are already seeing that in communications and the effect it has on our culture.
Here is the problem. Recently, one of my assistants went into a video store in Ottawa and looked at the foreign film section where he found not one but several Canadian films including Grey Fox, The Decline of the American Empire and other films. I think this symbolizes why this debate is so important. They are not foreign films. They are Canadian films.
As John Gray, the noted playwright and performer from Vancouver has written, and I quote: "Increasingly, American mass culture is being seen by Canadians as normal culture and Canadian mass culture as abnormal culture. Canadian artists have moved to the fringes of our own country". I think he puts it very well.
Karl Deutsch, in a famous thesis, has written that the test of nationhood is that more communications take place within a country than between that country and another. In many ways Canada is failing its test. I will continue my speech after the interruption from the Senate.

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should ensure that key communications tools, such as radio and television broadcasting, remain in Canadian hands.
November 7, 1989

Mr. Speaker, as I was saying before the interruption, many of our important cultural industries are foreign controlled and many others, such as private television stations, are controlled by Canadian corporations, but they merely serve as conduits for American cultural material. In other words, the majority of programs are American.
Look at the situation in our country-3 per cent of film profits stay in Canada; 97 per cent of film distribution is done by American and international companies. Of video cassette sales, 3 per cent are Canadian. Canadian publishers own 30 per cent of our market. Seventy-eight per cent of magazines sold in Canada are foreign; the rest are Canadian. There are more hours of U.S. newscasts available on Canadian television than there are Canadian newscasts.
In a newspaper ad last year the Friends of Canadian Broadcasting spoke of a typical Canadian child. This child spends over 80 per cent of her television time watching American programs. She spends as much time watching American programming as she does attending school.
The average teenager in this country spends about 24 hours a week watching television. The majority of that time for Anglophones, about 80 per cent, is spent watching foreign programming, and for Francophones about 50 per cent. Now our people have to be open to the world. We live in a global village as Marshall McLuhan, the great Canadian communicator, said. But we also have to have our people see Canada. As I said, Karl Deutsch said part of the role of keeping a nation together is that we can communicate with each other. We have a vigorous country and we have to be showing each other what other parts of the country are like. We also have a vigorous Canadian artistic community that is looking for opportunities to perform and to show their cultural creations to Canadians.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, we need vigorous government measures both to encourage the development of Canadian domestic industries and structural changes to limit foreign controls over our markets in broadcasting, telecommunications, publishing and so on.
Private Members' Business
A government in the past introduced a number of measures of this type, such as Bill C-54, in the mid-1970s to protect our publishing industry. It worked. There was an outcry at that. There was a lot of reaction by the Americans, but we held strong. But you need a government that has a lot of courage. That is not something that has been apparent with this particular government.
The Mulroney government has been indifferent to goals, sometimes hostile to these goals of Canadianizing our culture. I will give you some examples. The first example is the free trade deal. It was not supposed to affect Canadian culture. Do you recall the pamphlet that was put out at the time of the last election campaign? It was entitled "What's the big deal on free trade?" by Rick Salutin and Terry Mosher. I will just quote one of the pages because I think it puts it better than I can. The headline is, "I don't care much about Canadian culture. I watch a lot of American TV." And it goes on to talk about the problem there. It states:
Wait a minute. What's this got to do with Canadian popular singers?
After this deal, there won't be any new ones. The U.S. record companies up here who help Canadians get started, will close and move back to the States. Canadians who want recording careers will have to go down there like they used to do, and they'll have to sound like Americans if they want to make it.
I heard the deal says we have a right to support our culture.
It says that. But get this. If our policies to support our culture cost the Americans money here in Canada, then they can penalize us through their trade laws!
Come again?
For instance, let's say our government does something to help Canadian writers or Canadian recording companies.
Let me add to that, or Canadian film makers, which they had proposed to do before the deal.
All the Americans have to do is say that they lost some record or book sales in Canada, because of those policies. The U.S. gets the right to halt our fish or grain or manufactured goods from going to the States, until we stop helping our own artists.
That's ridiculous. It's our country and our culture. What can our government do to them if they act that way?
Nothing. Our government has already agreed to it. It's in the deal.
That puts it very well. That is the problem in the trade deal. The fact is, if I can be more technical, the Americans can take measures of equivalent commercial

November 7, 1989
Private Members' Business
effect if we interfere in their broadcasting, or in their film distribution, or in their magazine policies in Canada. That is giving up a lot of our sovereignty. That is one of the reasons that we have to change this trade deal.
The government has abandoned its film distribution policy. In contrast to the Broadcasting Act the government has rejected the key recommendations of the Standing Committee on broadcasting to protect the Canadian market. I will come back to that in a moment.
The Prime Minister himself recently has had meetings with the big international publisher, Robert Maxwell, over newspapers. I predict that we could easily become a satellite of not only other countries but of big communications multinationals once people like Rupert Murdoch and Robert Maxwell get control of Canadian newspapers.
All the Canadian government has to do is drop the 30 per cent requirement. I think it is 30 per cent, which is the limit of foreign ownership in newspapers. Once the government drops that then even our newspapers will be taken over. So look out The Globe and Mail, The Toronto Star, Southams, and some of those other people who treat us politicians so well.
The government has applied the Baie Comeau policy inconsistently. The Baie Comeau policy is a policy that states if there are takeovers in the United States of companies that have subsidiaries in Canada, then the Canadian companies have to be put up for sale to Canadians. In the New American Libraries case the government said, "We will just ignore and forget about that policy."
Let me give you a response to that the government should take. We believe in the New Democratic Party that there are Canadian firms that produce the overwhelming majority of Canadian cultural products, that we have a viable industry and that it is worth encouraging. We have to protect our culture.
People generally believe in an open-market system. In this world, as I have said, it is an open world. But even the most sophisticated countries, including the States, protect their own culture. We could get really stream-rolled by the American steamroller, if you like.
In film distribution Jack Valenti of the American film industry, the great lobbyist, a friend of the president,
came to Toronto last week and threatened Canadians. Basically he said, "You had better listen to us." They were bully-boy tactics from the American film industry, so that the Americans can still control 98 per cent of film distribution in Canada.
I introduced a bill which would make structural changes in this market. It would require that we change the current situation. In other words, we would give a slice of the market-I think it is about 15 per cent-to Canadian distribution companies. That is really radical. That is what we propose to do. This government backed away from it, tore up the bill and simply backed away in the face of the American threat.
We have to fund the public broadcasters adequately, the CBC in particular. This government has cut back since it came to power in 1984. In its first four years it cut back from its budget to the CBC of about $970 million to about $770 million to the CBC. We have seen another $140 million in cutbacks. The new management has great plans for the CBC. But we are still facing the possibility of cutting regional programming, cutting news, putting commercials on The National, and so on. We need a five-year plan for the CBC so that it has adequate funding and so that there is no political interference in the CBC, as we could have now when the managers have to ask for more money.
In book publishing, we need a vigorous enforcement of the Baie Comeau policy. We need distinctive Canadian laws on concentration of ownership in the mass media. We cannot let the mass media be owned by just a few people. We have to insist that they remain in Canadian hands.
On television programming, the CBC should be encouraged to produce 95 per cent Canadian content in drama. The private sector must produce 50 per cent Canadian content in prime time between seven o'clock and eleven o'clock. If the private sector does not do it, then we take the licenses away and we get other Canadians who will do it, who will be pleased to get into the private market.
In telecommunications, the Conservatives, supported I might say by the Liberals sometimes, are extending the realm of what we call "in hand services", Call-Net. The Call-Net case is a good example. They are starting to open the door to American giant telephone companies.
November 7, 1989

We need to maintain a distinctive Canadian phone system. Bill C-41, a new bill, will have, first, Canadian control over the Prairie telephone companies. We know what this government will do. It will deregulate it and telephone rates in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta will shoot up for the average person. That has to be stopped.
We need a status of the artists legislation in this country to support Canadian artists, to give them access to social services and at the same time to consider their particular tax situation. It was done in Quebec. It can be done in Canada as a whole.

There is also a problem in Quebec. The French network, especially the CBC's French network, must produce more programs than the English network, but with a smaller budget. Therefore, we see fewer and fewer quality television dramas in French. I am quoting Quebec's creative community. The coalition for the defence of the CBC's French services came to testify and told us that they were forced to work in the studio because outdoor settings cost too much.
It takes money and resources to rival Dallas. The CBC must have resources if it is to protect and promote francophone culture.

So we have to upgrade Radio-Canada as well.
I will conclude with this. I have talked about the intent of the motion, which is to deal with the Canadianization of key communications tools, radio and television. It is important that they remain in Canadian hands.
Herbert Marcuse, the deceased philosopher of the 1960s and 1970s, writing in Eros and Civilization had this to say about culture and art: "Art in its privileged connection to the unconscious is able to express and evoke thoughts, feelings and desires otherwise denied expression". The artist, as Marshall McLuhan said, really looks to the future. The rest of us live in a rear view mirror society. The artist in many ways is in the future.
The Canadian artist is in fact setting the stage for the future direction of Canadian society. That is why we have
Private Members' Business
to let our people see Canadian artists and appreciate Canadian artists, whether it is theatre, film, dance, writing, publishing, or journalism. They are all in then-own way Canadian artists. We have to make this available to Canadians.
We know in Canada that the public network, the CBC, is underfunded and cannot live up to Canadian content requirements. We know that the private sector is in fact not doing its job. That is what the Caplan-Sauvageau report said. We have to encourage it. This government has backed away in every instance from that.
A country where video stores advertise Canadian videos as foreign films better pull up its socks in terms of culture. This is a highly competitive world in culture as in every other matter. We have to take measures, as I have outlined here, in broadcasting, telecommunications, in the status of the artist, and in other ways to protect Canadian artists and Canadian culture and allow Canadians to communicate between themselves in this great country.

Mr. Speaker, this motion speaks to keeping tools of communication, that is radio and television, in Canadian hands. That is the text we were presented with in speaking to the motion of my colleague. I would suggest that it goes further into other areas of serious concern, and the first I would suggest is that of our artists.
It must be recognized in today's society-and the minister pointed that out most succinctly this morning- that if we do not recognize the status of the artists in Canadian society and give them their due respect and acknowledge through concrete earning power their right and place in society, we will never be able to promote who we are and what we are through the voice of the distinctive Canadian artistic talent that does express who we are in our society. I think it leaves us impoverished in many ways.
As Canadians we truly live in a culturally occupied country. Some 80 per cent of our publishing industry is in foreign hands, 97 per cent of films shown in Canada are foreign, 85 per cent of records and tapes are based on imported master tapes. In broadcasting, 71 per cent of all programs viewed by English speaking Canadians on television are produced by Americans. The figure is much lower in French speaking Canada, but as globalization takes place that will be impacted too.

Private Members' Business
Indeed, defining and enhancing Canadian culture goes far beyond radio and television. School books, audio-visual documents, videos, literary and general works, scholarly and specialized books and magazines are also key, everyday tools used to train and educate new generations of Canadians. They shape our collective imagination, build the myths that frame our destinies, develop our perceptions, attitudes, beliefs and behaviour, and influence our way of living. That is not to leave aside the whole culture of sports: Canadian football, rugby, soccer, lacrosse, and our two new baseball teams are making baseball viewing the fastest growing sport on our television sets, and of course there is Hockey Night in Canada. Without it, what would Saturday night in Canada be like for tens of thousands of Canadians? That is all part of the culture of Canada.
I believe they can be powerful means of asserting national unity and national identity, if we would have access to those cultural skills as portrayed in a variety of ways in our theatres, on our screens, and in our libraries.
The former publisher of Saturday Night, John MacFar-lane, has said it so well: "It is important as a country to make the distinction between importing merchandise and importing culture. Wearing foreign shoes and driving foreign cars won't make us any less Canadian, but without our own culture, we're nothing more than a colony".
The Tories used to believe this too. In 1932, Prime Minister Bennett when introducing the first Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act stated: "This country must be assured of complete control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference or influence. Without such controls, radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals, and without such control, it can never be the agency by which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened".
I am going to have to ask my colleague to take over, please.

Whatever happened to that strong Tory voice? Did Mr. Bennett's worst fears come true? Because, despite this firm conviction, foreign companies were able obtain an advantageous position in Canadian broadcasting?
In 1968, a new Broadcasting Act was introduced which clearly stated that the Canadian broadcasting system must be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada.
As a result, through the courageous Liberal Canadian public policy enacted between 1969 and 1973, foreign firms divested themselves of interest in 55 cable broadcast firms, 13 television stations, 10 radio stations, and one short wave transmitting station. Canadian buy-back transitions totalled almost $150 million. These events benefited the entire Canadian economy with broadcast earnings jumping by 700 per cent and before tax profits by 550 per cent between 1968 and 1973. The number of jobs available to Canadians also doubled. Today these Canadian firms are among the healthiest and most profitable in the country, using the cutting edge of technology and breaking new frontiers.
This government has said it is in favour of increasing Canadian control of our key cultural tools. I believe we must go even further than the motion of the hon. member for Port Moody-Coquitlam, for if we look at the government's record it is not encouraging. It has failed to include within a new broadcasting bill an 80 per cent Canadian ownership, a requirement which was recommended by both the Caplan-Sauvageau report and the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. As a result, I will be introducing an amendment that will provide for 80 per cent Canadian ownership requirement, which I hope this government will have the vision to accept.
It also caved in to the American scorched earth threats on book publishing, the most blatant example being the purchase of Ginn and Company, without full control being divested to Canadians. Canadians have 51 per cent equity but major decisions can be vetoed by the majority shareholders, the Americas. Many of our national cultural Crown corporations do not even require board members to be Canadian citizens. This I hope to remedy soon through a Private Member's Bill.

In conclusion, broadcasting and the daily press in Canada have almost entirely been controlled by Canadian owned firms. Through the years the goal of Canadian ownership has been continually upheld.
A 1985 film industry task force concluded that in sectors where foreign domination remains strong, publishing and film, Canadian works distributed by indigenous companies are confined to a marginal position in the market. These same Canadian companies are constantly troubled by problems of undercapitalization and financial instability which prevent them from responding to the social, economic and cultural needs of the country. Therefore control of the communications industry is the bedrock of Canadian cultural sovereignty.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian ownership of radio and television broadcasting in this country has been an issue of great concern for all Canadian governments ever since the first Canadian broadcasting legislation was introduced by a Conservative Government in 1932. Under that legislation, the radiobroadcasting spectrum was considered as being in the public domain and subjected to regulations in the public interest.
When he introduced the original radiobroadcasting legislation, the then Prime Minister R.B. Bennett stated, and I quote:
First of all, this country must be assured of complete Canadian control of broadcasting from Canadian sources, free from foreign interference of influence. Without such control radio broadcasting can never become a great agency for the communication of matters of national concern and for the diffusion of national thought and ideals, and without such control it can never be the agency by which national consciousness may be fostered and sustained and national unity still further strengthened.
These remarks may be even more fitting today than they were in 1932. The Legislator has tried, in the Canadian radiobroadcasting legislation, to keep up with the times.
As a reflection of the changes is media ownership Paragraph 3 (b) of the Broadcasting Act of 1968 which is still in force today provides that the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada.
An order is council containing the directives issued to the CRTC concerning the ability of some Canadian corporations to hold a broadcasting licence has further defined this section of the Act.
The motion under consideration today refers to the key communication tools of broadcasting companies operating in Canada. We are not dealing here with broadcasting companies which broadcast in countries other than Canada and whose signal Canadians can receive. This is altogether a different issue.
Clearly the Canadian Government could neither ensure that Canadians own and control broadcasting undertakings outside the country nor require that the latter hold a licence to broadcast programs aimed at Canadians.

Private Members' Business
The Government broadcasting policy is not to restrict access to foreign programs, but rather to ensure that the Canadian broadcasting system offers a satisfactory choice of high quality Canadian programs.
Mr. Speaker, the legislation introduced by this Government proceeds along those lines.
First, the Bill reconfirms the principle that the radio spectrum is public property and must be regulated in the interests of all Canadians.
It further states that the broadcasting system provides through its programming a public service essential to the maintainance and enhancement of national identity and cultural sovereignty.
Second, the legislation uses the wording of the 1968 Act, which provides that the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians.
Third, concerning the increasing use of non-Canadian programs in our broadcasting system, the legislation expressly empowers the CRTC to regulate the provision of programming services, even from foreign sources, by broadcasting undertakings.
Under that paragraph, Mr. Speaker, it would be the Commission's duty to strike the most appropriate balance between Canadian and foreign programs. In my view, this is an approach that a majority of Canadians would support.
The definition of "effectively owned and controlled by Canadians" would still be determined by the Governor in Council. This provides the Government with the flexibility needed to specify what is a Canadian corporation under the Act.
The current direction concerning Canadian corporations eligible to hold a broadcasting licence are contained in eight paragraphs covering two pages. Elowever, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture in June 1989 recommended that the direction be made more specific, in terms especially of the provisions concerning paid-up capital.
To show how complex that kind of regulations can be, I would like to read into the record parts of the current
direction, which was drafted to be as specific as possible. The direction starts at Section 2, and I quote:
The Canadian Radio Television and Telecommunications Commission is herby directed that, on and after January 12, 1971, broadcasting licences may not be issued and renewals of broadcasting licences may not be guaranteed to applicants of the classes described in Section 3.
Section 3. The classes referred to in section 2 are as follows:
(a)	persons who are not Canadian citizens or eligible Canadian corporations; and
(b)	governments of countries other than Canada or of political subdivisions of countries other than Canada and agents of such governments.
Section 4. For the purposes of this Direction, an "eligible Canadian corporation" is a corporation
(a)	that is incorporated under the laws of Canada or a province,
(b)	of which the chairman or other presiding officer and each of the directors or other similar officers are Canadians citizens, and
(c)	of which, if it is corporation having share capital, at least four-fifths of the shares having full voting rights under all circumstances and shares representing in the aggregate at least four-fifths of the paid-up capital are beneficially owned by Canadian citizens or by corporations other than corporations that are controlled directly or indirectly by citizens or subjects of a country other than Canada.
Except that, in any case where, in the opinion of the Commission, notwithstanding that the corporation is one to which subparagraphs (a) to (c) apply, the corporation is effectively owned or controlled either directly or indirectly and either through the holding of shares of the corporation or any other corporation or through the holding of a significant portion of the outstanding debt of the corporation or in any other manner whatever, by or on behalf of any person, body or authority of a class described in section 3, the corporation shall be deemed not to be an eligible Canadian corporation.
The Govemement has already stated its intention, Mr. Speaker, in the Broadcasting Bill to keep the legislative and regulatory provisions concerning Canadian ownership of the electronic media in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, broadcasting is perhaps the most important of our cultural industries. This legislation is part of the Government's commitment to protect and strengthen Canadian cultural sovereignty.

I was at a meeting of the Canada-U.S. Interparliamentary Group some two years ago. It was the Americans' turn to have the meeting and it was in Key West, Florida. I see my colleague across the way from Burlington who was also at the meeting. We were all discussing this issue with American legislators, congressmen and senators. They had been lobbied extensively before coming to the meeting by Jack Valenti. That was obvious. They even admitted to that in discussions that we had.
It was interesting that they all came into that meeting feeling how unfair Canadians were because we were restricting the Americans in their opportunity to invest in and to work in this field in Canada in a way that was unhindered, and that we should not put those unfair road blocks there, according to the senators and congressmen who had just been lobbied by Mr. Valenti.
In discussing this with them we asked one American congressman how he would feel if he watched film after film and never saw a place in his own country, never saw a scene where he had actually been in the country where he had lived all his life and where he was born. We asked: "Would you, as Americans, accept that?"

They said: "Of course not. That would be intolerable. We would not accept having only films from England in the United States. That just would not do".
We said: "Did it ever occur to you that 3 per cent of what we see in Canada is ours, only 3 per cent, and Jack Valenti is telling you that that is too much?"
They looked at it and said: "Maybe if you put it that way, I suppose it is worth looking at again."
What this tells me, apart from the fact that Mr. Valenti and others are extremely powerful lobbyists in the United States, is that they do not exactly give a straight bill of goods to American legislators. They do not represent the true facts to them. Therefore, often the only view that the American senator and congressman have of our country is that presented to them by these lobbyists with their own vested interests trying to control the whole industry.
We are not talking about something small here. We are talking about a $6 billion industry. We are talking about a lot of money. Therefore it is quite easy for lobbyists on the part of that industry to put out very glossy brochures and very effective and dramatic examples of some effort that we may have done to protect our Canadian culture and to exaggerate, way out of proportion and in very dramatic ways, to show their own government officials how we as Canadians according to them are unfair.
The only unfairness is the unfairness to our own citizens that we do not protect our culture enough in this country, and that we must be very vigilant in that regard. We must protect both the Canadian content itself and, not as some have said, just the container. We must protect the ownership of the industry. We must protect the availability of programming to Canadians. We must ensure that the decision-making ability remains Canadian as well.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REMOVAL OF OATS FROM CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-RESULTS OF DECIMA POLL
AGRICULTURE-REMOVAL OF OATS FROM CANADIAN WHEAT BOARD-RESULTS OF DECIMA POLL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rose in the House on May 4 last to question the Minister of Agriculture with respect to the future of the Canadian Wheat Board, particularly with respect to oats under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board which at that time had not yet been removed.
My question to the minister was this: If it could be demonstrated that a large majority of producers in western Canada did not want oats removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, would the minister heed those wishes and in fact would the minister allow the producers in western Canada to decide the future of their own Canadian Wheat Board?
The minister did not answer my question. Instead, he simply went on to state that there had been ongoing consultations.
In the supplementary part of the question he again did not answer but outlined some of the groups which had been consulted. These included, as reported in Hansard, the United Grain Growers Association, the Canadian Western Wheat Growers Association, the Western Barley Growers Association, the Prairie Canola Growers Association, the Alberta Pork Producers Development Board, the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, the Cattlemen's Association, the Manitoba Farm Business Association, the Manitoba Hog Producers Marketing Board, the Saskatchewan Marketing Board, the Government of Manitoba, the Government of Alberta and the Government of Saskatchewan.
It is all very well to have consulted these groups, but I am wondering what o these groups have to do with the future of oats under the Canadian Wheat Board.
With respect to the United Grain Growers and with respect to the Canadian Wheat Growers Association, it is valid to consult those groups because they in fact have oats producers with them. But I would like to know what
the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission has to do with the production of oats in western Canada.
Further, what does the Cattlemen's Association, the Manitoba Farm Business Association, the Manitoba Hog Producers Marketing Board and the Saskatchewan Marketing Board have to do with it? They do not grow oats. What does the Western Barley Growers Association and the Prairie Canola Growers Association have to do with it? They do not represent oats producers; they represent other commodities.
Mr. Speaker, what the minister failed to point out was that there had been a Decima poll that had just been completed at that time. The minister knew about it. That poll pointed out that well over 70 per cent of producers in western Canada felt that they had not been consulted on the oats issue. Furthermore, fully two-thirds of producers in western Canada wanted to have oats remain under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.
What the minister failed to point out was that the prairie wheat pools were not consulted, specifically the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which is probably the largest individual farm organization in the country and which opposed the removal of oats.
The minister did not indicate that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture actually passed a resolution at its last convention saying that oats should not be removed without a vote by the producers in western Canada. The minister did not even point out the fact that the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board had not been consulted. The Minister for Grains and Oilseeds has pointed out that he had no obligation to consult with the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board. The advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board is a democratically elected body representing some 140,000 permit book holders in western Canada. It is there to advise the wheat board.
It is true that the minister does not have to consult with the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board, but there is no obligation for him to consult with the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission either. I would think it is much more logical to consult with the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board than it is to consult with the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission with respect to the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board.

The reason there was no consultation with these other groups that I have mentioned is that they were opposed to the removal of oats from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. The government consulted only with those groups that agreed with its position and certainly not groups germane to the issue at hand, namely, the future of the Canadian Wheat Board.
I again would ask: Why does not the government allow the permit book holders in western Canada to decide the fate and the future of their own wheat board? It is a wheat board that is funded by producers, funded by farmers who are members of the Canadian Wheat Board. They should be deciding the future of that wheat board.
If the member who is going to respond on behalf of the government is simply going to spout some rhetoric and not answer the question, he need not bother, because farmers in western Canada are concerned about their future way of life. They see their way of life eroding and they see the Canadian Wheat Board as an integral part of that way of life.
I again ask this government, will it not allow the producers, the members, the permit book holders in western Canada, those 140,000 farmers, to decide their own fate and to decide the future of the Canadian Wheat Board?

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to confirm this government's commitment to consultation when making policy decisions. The commitment was met again when farm groups told us they wanted the responsibility for marketing oats transferred from the Canadian Wheat Board to the private individuals and co-operative companies.
We talked to farmers and farm groups about marketing oats for three years. As well as talking to producers and their organizations, we talked to traders, processors and provincial governments. We were told by many groups that they wanted the change in marketing. These groups included the United Grain Growers, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers Association, the Western Barley Growers Association, the Prairie Canola Growers Association, Alberta Pork Producers Development Corporation, the Alberta Sheep and Wool Commission, the
Adjournment Debate
Prairie Cattlemen's Association, the Manitoba Farm Business Association, the Manitoba Hog Producers Marketing Board, the Saskatchewan Pork Producers Marketing Board and the governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. So you can see the extent of our consultations.
In 1988-89 oats ranked sixth in value among the Canadian export crops and accounted for 4 per cent of the Canadian Wheat Board export sales. This was the peak year for Canadian oats exports because of the drought-reduced crop in the U.S.
Oats is a special crop sold in small quantities with specific quality requirements for human food and racehorse feed. Private traders have the flexibility both to pursue niche markets and to handle bulk sales of feed oats. This flexibility means oats producers will have a marketing system suited to their needs.
The change in the marketing does not affect the quotas, grading and weighing of oats handled by the elevator system. Grain companies and co-operatives will be able to offer pooled price options to producers as they do now with many other special crops. The change in oats marketing is not related to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement or any other international trade discussion. The decision was based on the merits of the product itself.
The U.S. demand for food oats is growing and Canada's reputation for producing high quality oats means new opportunities for Canadian oats producers. The new system is already providing increased opportunities for oats processing facilities on the prairies.
Can-Oat Milling Inc. recently introduced the building of an oats processing plant near Portage la Prairie, Manitoba, while Con-Agra and Westglen Mills are building a plant near Barrhead, Alberta, as a joint venture. Oats producers will be able to capture premiums offered in these markets.
I am confident this change to the marketing system is the best in the long-term interests of the producers.

Mr. Speaker, it pleases me to rise tonight under Standing Orders 37 and 38 to question the government on a vital matter of political reform.

November 7, 1989
Adjournment Debate
The House will recall that I raised, on October 30, the issue of the Alberta vacancy in the Senate. The Prime Minister had no answer, indeed seemed unprepared for the question, so I trust the government will have some kind of reply now.
Two years ago this seat became vacant with the resignation of Senator Cameron. It has been vacant since. The House will know how senators have traditionally been appointed and we are seeing some of the consequences of that now with Senator Cogger.
Since the early 1980s there has been a determined move to reform the Senate of Canada. It began in Alberta but since the advent of my party it has grown rapidly. It now is the position of all governments in western Canada, most in eastern Canada, and is gaining a foothold in parts of central Canada. This, of course, is the Triple-E movement. It is enshrined in the legal text of a constitutional amendment drawn up by a reform party sponsored task force and presented to the western premiers in May of 1988.
The idea is to make the Senate elected with an effective veto power over federal legislation and with equal representation from each province. Australia has such a Senate in a parliamentary system like ours and it has served to lessen the regional transfers and regional tensions that have characterized our federal system. In Canada, due to its undemocratic nature, the Senate has lacked the moral authority to fulfil the role of regional representation given it by the Fathers of Confederation.
It is truly unbelievable that in 1989 one quarter of the seats in the Parliament of Canada remain unelected. Indeed, many are reserved for patronage appointments of the worst kind. The irony of this is not lost on the Canadian voter as he gazes in disbelief at our Prime Minister pontificating about democracy on the international stage.
The Prime Minister decided to appoint senators from provincial lists under the terms of the unratified Meech Lake Accord. It is interesting to note that just yesterday, Premier Getty announced that he will rethink his position on Meech Lake if the Prime Minister continues to waver on appointing Mr. Waters. The Prime Minister and others did not count on the strength of the tide for Senate reform sweeping the west. And, as any sincere
Senate reformer knows, electing senators is the essence of any reform and certainly not an item for negotiation.
Premier Getty in Alberta wisely agreed to be guided by the electorate in submitting his choice to the Prime Minister. In August of this year, the Alberta legislature passed the Senatorial Selection Act to provide a legislative framework for the Premier's advice to the Prime Minister.
Hon. members will know clearly what happened. Despite the shrill warning of a few Tory MPs, Albertans went to the polls en masse on October 16 and voted overwhelmingly for Lieutenant-General Stanley C. Waters, the Reform Party candidate who garnered over 40 per cent of the votes. Liberal, PC, and Independent candidates trailed far behind. The NDP chose not to field a candidate. It is apparently the NDP view that socialism is ideologically incompatible with regional representation.
On October 19, Premier Getty submitted the list of candidates and their vote totals to the Prime Minister in order to satisfy the provisions of both the Meech Lake Accord and the Senatorial Selection Act. So that brings us to today. What is the Prime Minister to do? It is clear there are only two choices: first, he could appoint immediately the clear choice of Albertans, or second, use some other criteria.
I want to review, if I could, three of the red herrings used to argue against Mr. Waters' appointment to the Senate. The first is that the appointment should be delayed until the Meech Lake Accord is finished dying and wreaking its havoc upon federal-provincial relations in this country. This in no way prevents Albertans' clear choice being appointed to a seat that is vacant now.
The second argument is that Mr. Waters is politically unsuited to the position. Indeed, in the eyes of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, he should not be appointed because of his political views. Of course, it is precisely these political views upon which Mr. Waters was elected. Albertans had the option of the PC and turned it down. They wanted a candidate from a party to fight Meech Lake, enforced bilingualism but most of all to fight the goods and services tax and the reckless spending of this government. These views are not widely shared, perhaps, in Ottawa but that is the representation that Albertans want.

This is not only an undemocratic argument; it is also dangerous and untrue. Mr. Waters is a forthright man who shoots from the hip. Under the Trudeau administration, he was commander of the Canadian Army. Since retiring from the Forces, he has been one of Alberta's most prominent businessmen and, indeed, was a very prominent Tory until Preston Manning arrived on the scene. The External Affairs Minister's comments about Mr. Waters' views possibly say more about his own attitude to fiscal conservatives in his own party than they do about Mr. Waters.
Finally there is the argument that this series of events has somehow violated the Canadian Constitution. Let me make my party's position clear here. Under the Constitution Act, 1867, Section 24, it is the Governor General who appoints senators and the Governor General is free to do as he or she pleases. Now we know that the Governor General, by convention, takes advice from the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister may choose to recommend Mr. Waters or anyone else. That is his choice.
I would remind the government, however, that a constitution operates not only according to the letter of the law but also according to a series of conventions, the intention of which is to ensure that the democratic will prevails. Clearly, the Prime Minister has the technical authority to do what he wants, but the political culture of our country clearly says that the right thing to do is to appoint Mr. Waters and appoint him now. If he denies democracy or delays it, it will be clear where he stands with regard to the views of Albertans and their basic right to representation. I trust that whoever answers my question will shed some light on where the government really stands on this issue and Senate reform generally. The government has been suspiciously quiet about where it stands on every one of the three Es in the reform proposal. In both the debate over Meech Lake and over Mr. Waters it is becoming increasingly suggested by Canadians that the government is really trying to block Senate reform in almost any form. Perhaps this is what Premier Getty is beginning to suspect. It seems as though he is definitely concerned about that. Nothing radical is happening here. It is just a start. After 122 years, surely westerners are entitled to that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in an exchange with the Prime Minister on October 30, the member for Beaver River asked whether Canadians can expect to hear of the appointment of Stan Waters to the Senate of Canada.
As the hon. member is probably aware, Premier Getty wrote to the Prime Minister last October 19 while the Prime Minister was out of the country. In his response to the question last Monday, the Prime Minister indicated that he had not yet had an opportunity to consider the matter. Senate appointments remain the Prime Minister's prerogative. It is only reasonable that he have the time to do so.
The hon. member raised a second issue last Monday. She said, "It is not a matter of when but it is a matter of why not reform the Senate". I would like to take this opportunity to respond on behalf of the government.
In August, 1986, all premiers agreed to defer Senate reform to a second round of constitutional discussions when all governments would once again be present at the constitutional table. Once proclaimed, the Meech Lake Accord will guarantee that Senate reform will be a priority agenda item on future annual constitutional conferences by the First Ministers. The Government of Canada is committed to fundamental Senate reform. The Prime Minister has promised to table a proposal for an elected Senate in the first constitutional conference provided by the Meech Lake Accord.
In the meantime, to reflect the federal government's commitment to pursue this important issue, earlier this year Senator Murray carried out a round of informal bilateral consultations on Senate reform with all provincial governments. So, we share the hon. member's belief that there should be fundamental reform of the Senate. That being said, questions have been raised about Alberta's Senate election initiative.
As I see it, Alberta's initiative raises issues that go well beyond filling one Senate vacancy. It touches on the role of one of our two Houses of Parliament and the broad question of how we should go about reforming the Senate. Some commentators noted that a precedent could be created here. Some have said that this is a good precedent, and that they hope other provinces will adopt Alberta's process. Others, including Alberta Intergov-

Adjournment Debate
ernmental Affairs Minister, James Horsman, have said that they do not favour creating an elected Senate in a piecemeal way. Speaking in the legislative assembly last July 26, Mr. Horsman said that a danger inherent in Alberta's proposal was that: "if every province were to do this we could by about 2020 have entrenched in the Constitution of Canada an elected Senate with its current powers".
Mr. Horsman went on to say that no government in Canada would want to see that happen.
Mr. Horsman raised a legitimate concern. Would there not be implications for relations between the two Houses of Parliament if the Senate became an elected body with its current powers which are virtually equal to those of this House and remain untouched? It is a good question.
What would it mean if Ontario decided to elect Senators to fill its three current vacancies, and eventually Ontario and Quebec elected all 48 of their Senators? Having done this and entrenched their supremacy, what incentive would Ontario and Quebec have to talk about Senate representation and powers?
These are all legitimate questions that merit consideration in light of the national implications of this Alberta innovation. Senate reform is very important to the future of the federation. The federal government is committed to its pursuit following ratification of the Meech Lake Accord. However, it is a complex issue which raises a number of questions that might best be addressed together rather than one at a time as part of an effort to achieve reform in a piecemeal way.
